prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, and the experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B006 as my preferred configuration but I change the third name from Hasan to Mele, and I want to be explicit about why. In round 1 I made my support conditional on checking what Mele actually contributed. The chair's first question asks the same thing, and I have now worked through the record as it appears in the shortlist and in my colleagues' statements. Kane and Mele published the two 2005 papers together: the quantum spin Hall effect in graphene, and the Z2 classification that says why the helical edge states cannot be removed. The three-dimensional step, which is where Hasan's ARPES work was aimed, was predicted in the Fu, Kane and Mele paper of 2007, so Mele is on both the two- and three-dimensional predictions. I cannot honestly tell the committee that I am sure who did the original theoretical work if I separate him from Kane. On the experimental side, the original verification is Molenkamp's 2007 measurement of the quantized edge conductance in HgTe, and it is the decisive observation of the quantum spin Hall state. The topic is verified by transport and ARPES, independently reproduced for almost twenty years, and it changed how we search for materials. The prize would honour the original prediction and the original experiment, which is what the statutes ask of us. B006 also has the broadest support (seven of eight ballots ranked it, four in the top three), but I am not relying on the count. I rely on the fact that the claim and its confirmation are both firmly on the record. My preferred citation is worded to the quantum spin Hall effect and the HgTe observation, so that it describes what these three people actually did.
statement.case_against: The cost of this configuration is Hasan. The 3D ARPES discovery in Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 is an original experiment with the widest materials impact, and my round-1 trio recognised it. By choosing Kane, Mele and Molenkamp we leave that experiment without a laureate, and Fu, Moore, Balents and others on the 3D side are also outside the credit. I accept that cost because a three-name limit forces a choice and I would rather keep the theorists together than split Kane from Mele. The second weakness is Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal told Molenkamp what to measure and who cannot be credited because Zhang is deceased. A citation to the quantum spin Hall effect and the HgTe observation cannot fully close that gap. The third is the 2016 prize for topological phases of matter. I consider the question answerable, since the 2016 laureates dealt with topological phase transitions and quantized Hall-type invariants in model systems, whereas B006 concerns time-reversal-invariant topology in real materials, but the committee must argue it in the citation and not assume it. If the committee finds the credit still unresolvable, my fallback is B047 and not B017, for reasons given below.

responses.point: Mehlig argued that a prize built on Molenkamp and Hasan alone would credit the confirmations without the idea behind them, that Kane and Mele should stay with Molenkamp as the experimental anchor, and that if Hasan is kept the committee must say which theorist it gives up.
responses.response: He has persuaded me on the central point. I had supported Hasan because I weight the experiment, but the fair reading is that a prize crediting Kane without Mele makes a statement about origin that the 2005 papers do not support, and the Fu-Kane-Mele paper ties Mele to the 3D prediction as well. I move to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. I still differ from Bernhard in one respect. I do not think the loss of Hasan is a small detail, because his ARPES observation is an original experiment and not a later refinement. I would want the committee minutes to say plainly that this is a cut forced by the three-name rule and not a judgement on Hasan's work.

responses.point: Danielsson supports Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, calls B006 the most settled configuration on the shortlist, and recognises that Mele is inseparable from Kane for the theory and that the three-name limit forces a choice.
responses.response: Ulf and I held the same trio in round 1 and I now leave it. I agree with his reading of the maturity and with his view that the 2016 objection can be answered. Where I disagree is on the cost of the third seat. He treats it as dropping Mele or Hasan and accepts either. I now think the theory pair has the stronger claim to be kept together, because the 2005 papers were joint and the 3D prediction was also joint, whereas the 3D experiment was done by several groups at almost the same time. Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 were observed by ARPES in more than one laboratory, so the priority of a single experimental name is harder to defend than the priority of Kane and Mele. If he can show that Hasan's contribution to the 3D discovery is cleanly separable from the parallel ARPES work, I will listen, but my current view is that the attribution is more certain with Mele.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the optical lattice clock is a well-verified instrument advance with a clean two-name credit, that the magic-wavelength lattice is a new principle, and that the redefinition of the second does not need to come first because independent comparisons already settle the result.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing case and I have moved B047 to the top of my alternatives. In round 1 I asked whether the redefinition of the second was a precondition, and Stefan's answer, that independent comparisons at 1e-18 across JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST and SYRTE already settle the result, is persuasive to me as an experimentalist: reproducibility is the test I care about, and the redefinition is an administrative step that will follow from the measurement and not the other way round. What I still cannot settle is novelty relative to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. The magic-wavelength condition is a new principle and I accept that, but the discoveries so far are limits and precision, and the statutes ask for discovery or invention. I would call it an invention, and that is within our mandate, so I no longer regard it as disqualifying. Where I differ from him is the third seat: if the committee has doubts about the independent lattice groups, I would prefer to resolve this on the record and not by adding a name, since neither Lemonde nor the Yb groups have a clearer claim than Katori and Ye.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair and a supporter of B047, concedes that B006 has the widest support and would be the better fit if the committee wants the broadest consensus, at the cost of the four-names-into-three problem.
responses.response: I thank the chair for stating the trade-off so directly, and I do not want the committee to choose by counting. My answer to the chair's question about what would change my order is this. If B047 had the same number of members who regard it as a discovery, I would rank it first because its credit is cleaner. For now I judge B006 to be the stronger scientific case: a prediction that nature could have refused, followed by an original measurement, followed by twenty years of independent confirmation. B047 is a more certain attribution, B006 a more important discovery. The four-into-three problem is real, and my move to Mele is partly a response to it, because it removes the part of the problem that I think is worst, the separation of the two 2005 authors.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and asked me in round 1 to argue for B017 in round 2, and he noted that attribution and the 2007 overlap are serious problems for TMR.
responses.response: I will answer him honestly. I do not think B017 can be defended for this year. The quantitative prediction and the 2018 observation are real, and I admire the theory-experiment loop, but the pairing mechanism and device disorder are unresolved, and the credit goes to a group leader while Cao and Fatemi, who did the measurements, are outside it. For TMR, I withdraw it as a preferred position, since I could not show that the Parkin question can be resolved and nobody else ranked it. I keep B017 as an alternative because it is the best candidate for a later cycle.

uncertainties: Whether Hasan's 3D ARPES discovery can be separated cleanly from the parallel ARPES work in other laboratories, because if it can, the argument for crediting him in place of Mele would be stronger than I now think.
Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize leaves enough room for B006, and whether the citation as worded makes the distinction without overclaiming for the Z2 insulator.
Whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be defended in the citation, given that Zhang is deceased and the HgTe experiment followed their proposal.
Whether B047 should be preferred if the committee decides that the cleaner credit outweighs the broader support and that the lattice principle is a new invention distinct from the earlier prizes.
statement.conflict_note: My disclosure is unchanged. I have no personal conflict requiring recusal for B006 or for the credited names Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. Katori (B047, my first alternative) is at the University of Tokyo, where I have been a Fellow since 2025, and Miyazaki (B015) is at Tohoku University, where I lectured in 2026. Those are institutional contacts, not collaborations, and I have no joint publications with the names on my ballot or with Katori or Ye. Johansson, who prefers B038, is my Chalmers physics colleague and Mehlig is in the neighbouring Gothenburg department, which I record for transparency. None of these relationships bears on my position.
